evening.title: From Project Airavat to Netra: How India Spent Four Decades Building Its Indigenous AEW&C Capability
evening.text:
India’s indigenous airborne early-warning journey is one of the country’s longest and most difficult defence technology programmes. What is today represented by the Netra Airborne Early Warning and Control (AEW&C) system can be traced back to research efforts that began in the mid-1980s, followed by a devastating 1999 crash that killed eight personnel and temporarily halted the programme. The eventual revival of the effort demonstrates how India gradually moved from technology demonstration to a sophisticated operational airborne surveillance architecture.
The origins of the programme can be traced to 1985, when India began studying airborne early-warning technology under an effort associated with Project Guardian, subsequently known as Airavat. A DRDO newsletter published in 2017 records that national initiatives in airborne early warning began at BEL in 1985 and later continued through the Airborne Surveillance Platform programme at DRDO.
The initial challenge was enormous. India did not possess a purpose-built airborne surveillance aircraft or the indigenous technology required to integrate a sophisticated radar, signal processing, communications and command-and-control system onto an aircraft. The solution was therefore to develop the technology incrementally using an available platform.
This eventually led to the Airborne Surveillance Platform (ASP) based on the HS-748 Avro aircraft. The aircraft was modified with a large rotating radar dome, while DRDO organisations including the Centre for Airborne Systems (CABS) and Electronics and Radar Development Establishment (LRDE) worked on the airborne electronics and radar technology. CABS was established in 1991 and became the system house responsible for airborne electronic systems and integration.
The modified aircraft began flying with the radar-related modifications during the early 1990s. The programme was deliberately structured as a technology demonstrator rather than an immediately deployable operational AWACS. The objective was to acquire experience in airborne radar, signal processing, communications, integration and flight testing before attempting a more sophisticated operational system. Contemporary assessments noted that the ASP was intended as a first step towards a full-fledged airborne early-warning capability.
Then came the tragedy that changed the programme.
On 11 January 1999, the ASP prototype crashed near Arakkonam in Tamil Nadu during a test flight. All eight people aboard were killed, including four DRDO scientists and four Indian Air Force personnel. The crash brought the programme to an abrupt halt and became one of the darkest moments in India’s indigenous airborne surveillance effort. Parliamentary records subsequently recorded that the ASP project was formally short-closed in November 1999 following the accident.
The accident was particularly damaging because the programme had already accumulated considerable technical experience. Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam later recalled the Arakkonam crash as a devastating experience and spoke of the eight personnel who lost their lives in the scientific effort. His account also describes how the aircraft conducted radar trials along the Arakkonam-Chennai coastal region, highlighting the demanding nature of the flight-testing programme.
But India did not abandon the objective.
By the early 2000s, DRDO began rebuilding the programme around a new architecture. The revived effort moved away from the Avro platform and eventually selected the Embraer EMB-145 regional jet as the flying platform. This represented a major philosophical and technological transition. Instead of attempting to turn an ageing transport aircraft into a complete operational AEW&C system, India could concentrate on developing an indigenous mission system around a more suitable modern aircraft.
The programme was revived in 2004, with CABS taking the lead in developing the indigenous mission system. DRDO’s own account identifies 2004 as the year in which the AEW&C programme was restarted, eventually leading to the Netra system.
The new architecture also reflected lessons learned from Airavat. India increasingly treated the aircraft not simply as a modified airframe carrying a radar, but as an integrated system of systems involving radar, electronic support measures, communications, data links, mission computers, operator consoles and command-and-control functions.
The result was the Netra AEW&C, with DRDO developing the mission system and associated technologies while integrating them onto the Embraer platform. After years of development and testing, the system eventually entered operational service and became a key component of India’s airborne surveillance architecture.
The journey reached another important milestone in June 2026, when DRDO and the IAF declared Final Operational Clearance for the indigenous Netra AEW&C system. The FOC ceremony was dedicated to the eight scientists and air warriors who died in the 1999 ASP crash, providing a remarkable connection between India’s earliest airborne-surveillance experiment and its eventual operational achievement.
The significance of Netra therefore goes far beyond the aircraft itself. India’s current AEW&C capability is the product of four decades of accumulated institutional knowledge—from Airavat and the Avro demonstrator, through the painful lessons of Arakkonam, to the development of indigenous radar, mission computing, communications and sensor integration.

evening.title: The Battle Beneath the Waves: India’s Dangerous Seabed Warfare Gap
evening.text:
In July 2026, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) floated an expression of interest that should have made headlines. The Naval Physical and Oceanographic Laboratory (NPOL) in Kochi — India’s premier underwater warfare lab — began searching for an industry partner to build what it called an Underwater Fibre Optic Sensing System (UFOSS), a fixed network of seabed sensors linked by subsea fibre-optic cables to a shore station. The project, internally referred to as “Deep Ocean Watch,” would cover the Ninety East Ridge, the Bay of Bengal, and waters around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands — the exact routes that Chinese and Pakistani submarines would transit to enter the Indian Ocean. (Source: New Indian Express, 5 July 2026; India Sentinels, 6 July 2026)
It is the first public move toward what could eventually become India’s underwater equivalent of the Iron Curtain — a permanent, seabed-based acoustic and electromagnetic barrier to detect, classify, and track every submarine, unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV), and surface vessel that enters Indian waters. The EOI specifies sensor array nodes, subsea fibre-optic cables, junction boxes, branching units, and a beach manhole connecting to a shore-based control facility. The selected lead system integrator will be responsible for the entire turnkey project — design, deployment, commissioning, one year of operations, and lifecycle support for a planned 20-year service life. Execution is tentatively pegged at 48 months. Proposals are due by September 1, 2026. (Source: New Indian Express; India Sentinels)
The problem is that 48 months from contract signing — assuming the RFP is issued, a bidder is selected, and the project proceeds without the delays that have characterised every major Indian defence programme — means India’s seabed sensor network will not be operational until at least 2031. And by then, the adversary will not have been standing still.
The Five-Layer Wall: China’s Transparent Ocean
While India has been debating the merits of indigenous versus imported fighter jets, China has been quietly building the most ambitious undersea surveillance architecture in human history. Publicly known as the “Transparent Ocean” program — first outlined by oceanographer Wu Lixin in 2014 — it aims to render the ocean fully transparent to Chinese sensors across the western Pacific, Indian Ocean, and South China Sea. (Source: Defense One, 15 October 2025; ABC News Australia, 16 May 2026)
The system, now operational in the South China Sea and expanding outward, consists of five interconnected layers, each spanning from the seabed to space:
China’s Blue Ocean Information Network — Five Layers
1. The Ocean Star Cluster (Space): A satellite constellation built around the Guanlan radar altimetry and ocean-profiling LIDAR system, which uses pulsed laser signals to generate high-resolution three-dimensional maps of the ocean surface and subsurface for wide-area cueing.
2. The Air-Sea Interface (Surface): Smart buoys, wave gliders, and unmanned surface vessels (USVs) that hold station across vital straits and continental shelves. They sample the upper ocean and serve as critical data relays, translating slow underwater acoustic data into high-bandwidth satellite bursts.
3. The Starry Deep Sea (Water Column): Deep floats, long-range gliders, and autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) that patrol below the mixed layer for weeks, profiling the ocean environment and towing acoustic payloads to fill the gaps identified by the orbital layer.
4. The Undersea Perspective (Seabed): The backbone of the entire grid. Fixed seabed observatories and cabled hubs host passive acoustic arrays, precise clocks, and navigation beacons. They provide docking, data offload, and recharging for visiting UUVs, allowing unmanned submarines to loiter and redeploy without surfacing — drastically extending endurance.
5. The Deep Blue Brain (AI Core): An artificial intelligence and data management system that integrates information across all domains, creating a real-time, automated “kill web” that can cue weapons systems without human intervention.
This is not a concept. It is a deployed, operational system. The Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative (AMTI) has confirmed that the Blue Ocean Information Network is concentrated in the northern South China Sea, stretching between Hainan Island’s Lingshui County and the Paracel Islands, with floating and fixed “Ocean E-Stations” monitoring critical chokepoints like the Qiongzhou Strait. Official Chinese plans call for expanding coverage across the rest of the South China Sea, into the East China Sea, along the Maritime Silk Road, and eventually into polar waters and — critically — the Indian Ocean. (Source: AMTI, CSIS, June 2020; Asia Times, 3 March 2026)
In August 2025, during the PLA Navy and Russia’s Joint Sea-2025 exercises near Vladivostok, Chinese and Russian forces linked their communications and shared hydro-meteorological and air-sea tracks in real time during anti-submarine warfare drills. Chinese state media described the goal as leaving deep-diving submarines with “nowhere to hide.” It was the first public demonstration of a mature, automated kill web that China plans to spread across multiple seas and oceans. (Source: Defense One)
The Indian Ocean Push
China’s seabed intelligence programme is already active in India’s backyard. Since 2022, a growing flotilla of Chinese “research” vessels — including the Shi Yan 6, Da Yang Hao, Da Yang Yi Hao, Dong Fang Hong 3, and others — have been systematically mapping the Indian Ocean seabed. In March 2026, three Chinese survey vessels were simultaneously active in the Indian Ocean Region, with the Shi Yan 6 operating near the Ninety East Ridge before docking at Malé, Maldives. (Source: Telegraph India, 25 March 2026; Cāṇakya, 26 March 2026; Indian Defence News, 1 April 2026)
The pattern is not accidental. These vessels return to the same locations repeatedly, building layer upon layer of bathymetric, acoustic, and environmental data. The Shi Yan class focuses on seabed mapping with sub-bottom profilers, magnetometers, and multibeam echo sounders. The Da Yang class drills into the sub-surface to analyse what lies beneath. Together, they are compiling the kind of detailed oceanographic intelligence that is directly applicable to submarine navigation, concealment, and the positioning of seabed sensors or weapons. (Source: Cāṇakya; Reuters Investigations, 24 March 2026)
A 2025 study by the French radio-frequency detection firm Unseenlabs identified nearly 1,900 vessels in the Bay of Bengal over a 16-day maritime surveillance survey. Approximately 10 per cent displayed suspicious behaviour, including switching off AIS tracking. Some were detected within 120 nautical miles of India’s coast, with indications of seabed mapping and underwater reconnaissance. (Source: The Print, 13 April 2026)
According to ORF, around 80 per cent of the 64 Chinese research and survey vessels active in the IOR are presumed to have organisational links to the PLA. At least 13 of these vessels have undertaken comprehensive surveys of the Indian Ocean’s underwater terrain. (Source: ORF, 19 March 2026)
Rear Admiral Mike Brookes, testifying before the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission, warned that China views undersea warfare as central to “systems confrontation” — integrating air, surface, seabed, and undersea sensors into a networked architecture to control key maritime areas and compel adversary submarines to withdraw. (Source: Asia Times)
India’s Shrinking Window
The strategic picture India faces in the undersea domain is bleak. According to the ORF, China has roughly doubled the number of submarines it rotates through the Indian Ocean Region since 2020. Yuan-class diesel-electric boats and Jin-class ballistic missile submarines have been tracked operating within range of Indian waters. (Source: ORF; News18, 26 March 2026)
Pakistan, meanwhile, is rapidly modernising its submarine fleet. The first of eight Chinese-built Hangor-class diesel-electric submarines with air-independent propulsion (AIP) — PNS Hangor — arrived in Karachi in June 2026. AIP technology allows these submarines to stay submerged for weeks without surfacing, a capability that Indian submarines still lack. Pakistani naval officers have publicly suggested that the Hangor could eventually operate as far away as the Bay of Bengal — a claim that, if realised, would add a second front to India’s undersea concerns. (Source: New Indian Express; India Sentinels)
India’s own underwater modernisation is years away from bridging the gap. The Navy does not currently operate a nuclear-powered attack submarine (SSN). The lease of the Russian Akula-class Chakra III has been delayed by more than three years. The indigenous programme to build two SSNs, cleared by the Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) in October 2024 at an initial cost of approximately ₹40,000 crore, is expected to take well over a decade before the first boat enters service. The Project-75I programme for six advanced conventional submarines has yet to receive CCS’s final approval — and even after the contract is signed, the first submarine is unlikely to be delivered for around seven years. (Source: New Indian Express)
With a depleted and ageing conventional submarine fleet and a shrinking ASW helicopter inventory, the Navy leans on a layered grid of P-8I maritime patrol aircraft, MH-60R multi-role helicopters, warships, and surveillance systems. Fixed seabed sensors like UFOSS are designed to plug a critical gap in that grid — but they are years from deployment.
The Infrastructure That Cannot Defend Itself
The vulnerability extends beyond military platforms. India’s digital economy — projected to exceed $1 trillion in value — rests on a network of approximately 18 international submarine cables landing at 23 stations concentrated across just five cities: Mumbai, Chennai, Kochi, Tuticorin, and Thiruvananthapuram. The Mumbai coastline alone acts as the gateway for 95 per cent of India’s international bandwidth. (Source: Carnegie Endowment, 23 July 2026; Stronger India, 15 April 2026)
Three new cable systems — 2Africa Pearls, India-Asia-Express, and India-Europe-Express — are expected to quadruple India’s international bandwidth, deepening this dependence even as it expands capacity. (Source: National Maritime Foundation, 2 June 2026)
Yet India has zero cable repair vessels that are Indian-flagged, Indian-owned, or permanently stationed within Indian maritime zones. When a cable breaks, India depends entirely on foreign repair fleets mobilising from depots in Singapore or the UAE — a dependence that produces repair timelines of four to five months on average. During periods of geopolitical tension, foreign commercial vessels may refuse to enter high-risk maritime zones. As the Takshashila Institution’s July 2026 discussion paper on subsea cable governance bluntly states: “India’s ability to restore its cables during a conflict or coordinated hybrid attack is, under current arrangements, virtually non-existent.” (Source: Takshashila Institution, 20 July 2026; The Print)
The disruption is not hypothetical. In September 2025, major cable disruptions took place across India, Pakistan, and West Asia. In February 2024, three main cables — AAE-1, SEACOM, and EIG — were cut, with one taking five months to repair because of regional dangers. The disruptions slowed financial systems, disrupted communications, and imposed considerable economic costs across the region. (Source: The Print)
The cost of inaction is already quantifiable. The disruption of undersea cables in Egypt and Dubai in 2008 caused India a loss of 80 per cent of international services over two weeks. India’s services economy is roughly ten times larger today. Establishing cable protection zones, converting two naval vessels for repair capability, and formally designating landing stations as critical national infrastructure is deliverable for under ₹5,000 crore. (Source: Stronger India)
The Legal Vacuum
The legal framework protecting this infrastructure is equally threadbare. The Indian Telegraph Act of 1885 — a colonial-era statute — cannot serve as a security doctrine for undersea cable protection. The Telecommunications Act of 2023 creates a modern framework for licensing and regulation, and extends extra-territorial criminal jurisdiction for damage to submarine cables. But the physical security layer — no repair ships, no protection zones, no unified command — remains unaddressed. (Source: Stronger India; National Maritime Foundation)
The National Maritime Foundation, in a March 2026 analysis, examined two recent cases of suspected cable sabotage — the Eagle S case in Finland and the Hong Tai 58 case in Taiwan — and found that successful prosecution hinged on factors India has not yet operationalised: declaring infrastructure as “critical” to support broader legal interpretation, publishing cable routes and protection zones, and maintaining the monitoring capability to apprehend vessels before they leave Indian waters. In the Hong Tai case, conviction was achieved because the vessel was apprehended before it could escape. In the Eagle S case, the vessel was acquitted. (Source: National Maritime Foundation, 29 March 2026)
The NMF recommends that India declare at least its national cables connecting the island chains as “critical infrastructure” — a step that would give courts broader interpretive latitude and enable security enforcement measures such as paramilitary deployment to cable landing stations, protected cable zones, and a “Green Channel” for repair vessel access. (Source: National Maritime Foundation)
What a Seabed Warfare Doctrine Looks Like — Elsewhere
The United Kingdom faced the same gap and moved with urgency. In January 2023, the UK Ministry of Defence purchased a commercial offshore support vessel, MV Topaz Tangaroa, for £70 million. After conversion at the Cammell Laird shipyard in Birkenhead, she was commissioned as RFA Proteus — the Royal Navy’s first dedicated Multi-Role Ocean Surveillance Ship (MROSS) — in October 2023. (Source: US Naval Institute Proceedings, February 2025; Royal Navy; DE&S)
RFA Proteus — The Model India Lacks
RFA Proteus is a 6,133-tonne, 98-metre vessel crewed by 26 RFA officers and sailors augmented by 60 Royal Navy specialists responsible for undersea surveillance, survey, and warfare systems. Her capabilities include:
- A 120-tonne active heave-compensation crane with a 3,000-metre wire for deploying payloads to the seabed
- A 7.2 m² moonpool for launching and recovering UUVs in protected conditions
- A 1,000 m² working/cargo deck capable of carrying up to 1,400 tonnes
- A hangar for ROVs and UUVs with workshops and launch-and-recovery systems
- A flight deck capable of launching helicopters up to 12,700 kg
- Dynamic positioning capability with five thrusters for holding station over precise seabed locations
- Three Kongsberg HUGIN Large UUVs capable of operating at depths of 6,000 metres
Proteus serves as both an operational platform and a floating testbed for new seabed warfare technologies. She was purchased, converted, and commissioned in under 11 months. (Source: USNI Proceedings; Naval News; Wikipedia)
The UK purchased Proteus at pace because the Nordstream pipeline attack in 2022 was, in the words of First Sea Lord Admiral Sir Ben Key, “a wake-up moment about the vulnerability of the critical national infrastructure on the seabed.” He added: “Whether carrying gas, electricity, or the data so vital to our economy, these cables and pipelines criss-cross every bit of the seabed around the United Kingdom, and travel far beyond under the high seas that make up two-thirds of the world’s oceans and are neither governed nor controlled by any one body.” (Source: Naval News, October 2023)
India has no equivalent vessel. No Indian ship is configured to deploy and recover UUVs, monitor the seabed, inspect cable infrastructure, or respond to subsea sabotage. The Navy has diving support vessels that could be converted for cable repair operations — the platforms exist. The order to convert them does not. (Source: Stronger India)
The Missing Indian Architecture
The ORF, in a July 2026 analysis titled “The Dark Ocean Challenge,” argued that undersea warfare is shifting from a platform-centric endeavour to one centred on subsea information networks, supported by a combination of crewed and uncrewed platforms. For India, this signifies an immediate need to shift towards a hybrid undersea force structure underpinned by a coherent Underwater Domain Awareness (UDA) architecture. (Source: ORF, 23 July 2026)
The challenge is twofold. On one hand, India must contend with a far more capable adversary in China, which is developing a unified approach that links strategy, naval modernisation, seabed infrastructure, and resource extraction into a single, connected effort — as described by a senior US naval officer. On the other, Pakistan may operationalise an asymmetric strategy using one-way attack drones procured from partner countries. India’s position is especially precarious given the close naval ties between Beijing and Islamabad. (Source: ORF)
The ORF’s prescription is that India should not merely invest in systems and technology, but develop a unique UDA architecture that connects a hybrid naval force structure to an undersea sensing network. Key recommendations include:
- Cooperation within regional UDA networks: The Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Cooperation Initiative mentioned by the four Quad countries, plus partnering with European nations to build something akin to NATO’s Digital Ocean Initiative and Critical Undersea Infrastructure Network.
- UUV co-development initiatives: Similar to AUKUS Pillar II, under which the US, UK, and Australia are developing payloads and enabling systems for uncrewed undersea vehicles.
- Common standards for data sharing and testing: Without which allied systems cannot interoperate in the undersea domain.
- A dedicated seabed warfare platform: Commissioning a dedicated seabed warfare ship comparable to the UK’s RFA Proteus, serving as a platform for autonomous underwater vehicles. Additionally, equipping Kalvari-class submarines for enhanced monitoring roles and developing an autonomous UUV picket at strategic chokepoints. (Source: ORF; Takshashila Institution)
The Sagar Initiative and Information Sharing
India is not starting from zero. The Indian Navy has been building cooperative maritime security frameworks. It designated an Offshore Patrol Vessel as Indian Ocean Ship (IOS) Sagar, which sailed with a multinational crew from nine Indian Ocean island and coastal states. The deployment included the first Africa–India Key Maritime Engagement (AIKEYME), co-hosted by India and Tanzania, focused on maritime security and information sharing. India is reaching out to partners to establish National Maritime Information Centres (NMICs) and is offering NISHAR — the Network for Information Sharing — a low-cost connectivity tool that uses terrestrial networks and INMARSAT to link shore-based centres, ships, and aircraft. (Source: National Maritime Foundation)
The Information Fusion Centre for the Indian Ocean Region (IFC-IOR), hosted by the Indian Navy and linked with the Information Management and Analysis Centre (IMAC), already fuses and disseminates maritime data from partner countries. But ORF notes it continues to face challenges in integrating other initiatives, limiting comprehensive information dissemination. The system needs to shift from “information sharing to enhancing operations through prediction.” (Source: ORF)
Yet all of this is surface-centric. The most sensitive dimensions of the maritime domain lie underwater, and India’s UDA architecture remains the missing layer.
The UFOSS Programme: What We Know
The Underwater Fibre Optic Sensing System, if it proceeds, would represent India’s first permanent seabed surveillance grid. According to the EOI and reporting by India Sentinels, the system’s key elements include:
Deep Ocean Watch — Programme Details
Coverage areas: The Ninety East Ridge (a 5,000-km submerged mountain chain from the Bay of Bengal towards the Southern Ocean), the Bay of Bengal, and waters around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands — all critical submarine transit routes between the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
Shore station: Kochi, serving as the nerve centre. The facility will include integration bays, acoustic analysis systems, automated reporting tools, and secure data storage for near-real-time processing.
Sensor types: Passive sonar hydrophones to detect propeller and machinery noise without revealing the listening system’s position. Crucially, the system will also include superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) — sensors capable of detecting the faint electromagnetic signals emitted by a submarine’s metal hull and machinery, even when the vessel is running silently.
Predecessor: DRDO’s Naval Science and Technological Laboratory has already trialled smaller seabed sensor suites — hydrophones, pingers, and junction boxes wired to shore-based control rooms — and demonstrated the ability to track underwater vehicles in a defined area. Deep Ocean Watch scales this proof of concept into a network covering hundreds of kilometres.
Conceptual model: Indian planners have long studied the US-Japanese “Fish Hook” system — an underwater listening chain stretching from Japan through Southeast Asia that has quietly tracked submarine movements for decades. The US deployed the Sound Surveillance System (SOSUS) during the Cold War. China has built its own “Underwater Great Wall.” UFOSS is India’s attempt to join this club. (Source: India Sentinels)
The SQUID sensors are particularly significant. Traditional passive sonar detects the acoustic noise of a submarine’s propeller and machinery. But modern submarines — particularly AIP-equipped boats like Pakistan’s Hangor class — are extraordinarily quiet, making acoustic detection increasingly difficult. SQUIDs detect the magnetic anomaly created by the ferromagnetic mass of a submarine’s hull, regardless of how silently it operates. This makes them one of the few sensor types that can detect modern ultra-quiet submarines, and their inclusion in the UFOSS architecture suggests DRDO is thinking beyond legacy sonar paradigms.
The challenge, however, is not sensor design. It is everything else: the cable-laying ships to deploy hundreds of kilometres of subsea fibre-optic cable, the remotely operated vehicles to bury and maintain them, the junction boxes rated for decades of service on the seabed, the shore station infrastructure, and the data fusion algorithms to process the torrent of acoustic and electromagnetic data. The EOI requires the lead system integrator to have proven expertise across subsea cable manufacturing and deployment, underwater systems, marine surveys, system integration, and shore monitoring stations — backed by dedicated cable-laying ships, ROVs, and cable burial ploughs. (Source: New Indian Express)
This is the same industrial ecosystem India lacks for civilian cable repair. The military and civilian gaps are the same gap.
The Cable-Repair Vessel Paradox
The Takshashila Institution’s July 2026 paper makes a point that should be obvious but apparently is not: the same capabilities needed to repair a broken undersea cable — cable-laying ships, ROVs, cable burial ploughs, marine engineering expertise — are the capabilities needed to deploy and maintain a seabed sensor network. India’s lack of indigenous cable repair vessels is not just a civilian telecommunications problem. It is a national security problem that directly constrains DRDO’s ability to deploy UFOSS. (Source: Takshashila Institution)
The Telecommunications Consultants of India produced a study proposing a procurement budget of ₹3,000 to ₹4,000 crore for indigenous cable repair vessels. The Department of Telecommunications has the study. The National Security Council Secretariat has the working group. The Navy has vessels awaiting conversion orders. The cables fault monthly and the repair ships remain unbuilt. (Source: Stronger India)
TRAI, India’s telecom regulator, has issued detailed recommendations including critical infrastructure status for submarine cable landing stations, essential services status for cable repair, a committee to work on financial viability models for India-flagged repair vessels, and a dedicated section in the Indian Telecommunications Bill to protect cable infrastructure. None of these have been operationally implemented. (Source: Stronger India; The Print)
A Roadmap — If India Chooses to Move
The pieces of a solution exist in scattered form across multiple think tank analyses, government studies, and DRDO tender documents. What is missing is the political will to treat the seabed as a defence priority on par with the air, land, and space domains.
1. Designate — Immediately
The Department of Telecommunications should coordinate with the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre to formally notify cable landing stations and submarine cables as Critical Information Infrastructure. This requires a policy decision, not a budget allocation. It unlocks security enforcement measures: paramilitary deployment to CLSs, protected cable zones, and a Green Channel for repair vessel access. (Source: Takshashila Institution; Stronger India)
2. Build the Ships
India needs at least two Indian-flagged cable repair vessels — and at least one dedicated seabed warfare platform modelled on RFA Proteus. The Navy has diving support vessels that could be converted for cable repair operations. The conversion order must come from the Ministry of Defence, with the Ministry of Communications as co-signatory. The UK purchased, converted, and commissioned RFA Proteus in 11 months for £70 million. There is no reason India cannot move at similar pace — if the order is given. (Source: Stronger India; USNI Proceedings)
3. Declare Protection Zones
Use the Telecommunications Act of 2023 to declare no-anchor, no-trawl zones around cable landing stations and key cable routes — particularly the six-kilometre Versova corridor that carries Mumbai’s international bandwidth. Australia did this in 2005. The Indian Coast Guard and state marine police can enforce these zones as part of the existing layered coastal security system. (Source: Stronger India)
4. Fast-Track UFOSS — and Integrate It
DRDO’s UFOSS must move from EOI to RFP to contract on an accelerated timeline, and the resulting sensor network must be integrated with the Navy’s existing ASW grid — P-8I aircraft, MH-60R helicopters, warships, and the IFC-IOR fusion centre. The system must also be integrated with India’s space-based surveillance architecture. The SBS-III constellation of 52 satellites, approved at ₹26,968 crore, will provide the space-based ISR layer. UFOSS provides the seabed layer. The gap is the integration — the command-and-control architecture that fuses satellite data, seabed sensor data, and ASW platform data into a single operational picture. (Source: Times of India, 21 July 2026; Daily Tips, 13 May 2026)
5. Build the International Coalition
The NMF has proposed a jointly operated seabed monitoring pilot along two critical Indo-Pacific corridors — provisionally the India-Singapore cable corridor and the India-Mauritius-South Africa corridor — combining distributed acoustic sensing, UUV-enabled inspection, and satellite integration. India would lead the technical framework and invite corridor partners to contribute sensing assets and data-sharing arrangements. (Source: National Maritime Foundation)
India should also seek to join or establish UUV co-development initiatives similar to AUKUS Pillar II. The Quad’s Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Cooperation Initiative is a ready framework. Without common standards for data sharing and testing, allied systems cannot interoperate in the undersea domain. (Source: ORF)
6. Develop a Seabed Warfare Doctrine
None of the above works in isolation. India needs a formal seabed warfare doctrine — a document that defines the seabed as an operational domain, assigns responsibility for its defence, establishes rules of engagement for subsea threats, and integrates seabed operations with the broader maritime, cyber, and space warfare frameworks. The UK moved on this after Nordstream. Australia moved after discovering Chinese sensors near the Lombok Strait. India has had its own wake-up calls — the 2024 and 2025 cable cuts, the Chinese survey vessels in the Bay of Bengal, Operation Sindoor’s surveillance gaps — but has not yet produced the doctrine.
The Cost of Delay
Every month that passes without a seabed warfare capability is a month in which Chinese survey vessels continue mapping the Indian Ocean floor, Chinese submarines continue refining their transit routes, and Pakistan’s AIP submarines settle into operational service. The data China is collecting now — bathymetry, thermoclines, salinity profiles, acoustic propagation models — is cumulative and irreversible. Each survey pass increases the resolution of their operational map. Once that knowledge is acquired, it cannot be unlearned.
In undersea warfare, environmental knowledge is often more decisive than platform capability. A submarine commander who knows the terrain, the sound propagation characteristics, and the thermal layers can hide where an adversary cannot find them. China is acquiring that knowledge now, systematically, across the Indian Ocean. India is still at the EOI stage. (Source: Cāṇakya)
The ORF’s warning is stark: “Unless India leverages its strategic partnerships to co-develop uncrewed naval systems and establish a unified undersea domain awareness architecture in the IOR, the undersea security environment is likely to deteriorate. A new era of undersea and seabed warfare is imminent for New Delhi — one that is sure to challenge the status quo of conventional naval strategy and fleet design.” (Source: ORF)
The seabed is a battlefield. India has the technology, the industrial base, and the maritime tradition to contest it. What it lacks is a doctrine, a ship, and the urgency to act before the window closes.

evening.title: From Zero Buyers to a Global Queue: How BrahMos Became India’s Hottest Export
evening.text:
In 2022, nobody wanted India’s BrahMos missile. Now the Philippines has it, Vietnam’s deal is signed, Indonesia is next, the UAE is in talks, and even Russia wants it. Operation Sindoor turned the missile into a global brand — and China is furious.
The transformation is staggering. Until 2022, the BrahMos — the world’s fastest supersonic cruise missile, jointly developed by India and Russia — had zero foreign buyers. Today, it has two contracted customers, a third in the pipeline, and at least half a dozen countries in the queue.
The breakthrough came at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore on 30 May 2026, when Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed what had been rumoured for years: “My understanding is that with both Indonesia and with Vietnam, the deal is in the final stages. In fact, for Vietnam, I understand that it has already been signed, probably not publicly announced, but it’s already been signed.”
The China Connection
The buyers’ list has a discernible pattern — and it is not accidental. The Philippines, Vietnam, and Indonesia are all locked in maritime disputes with China in the South China Sea. Each has turned to the BrahMos as a “carrier-killer” to stiffen deterrence against Beijing’s expanding naval presence. China has previously objected to such sales as interference in disputed waters. (Source: New Indian Express; The Diplomat)
The strategic logic is simple. The BrahMos flies at Mach 2.8 — nearly three times the speed of sound — with a range of 290 km (capped by MTCR guidelines for export). It can be launched from land, ships, submarines, and Sukhoi-30MKI fighters. Its speed and low-altitude terminal flight profile make interception extraordinarily difficult. For countries facing the Chinese Navy, it is the ultimate anti-access weapon. (Source: The Week, 30 May 2026)
The Operation Sindoor Effect
What turbocharged the export pipeline was combat performance. During Operation Sindoor in May 2025, BrahMos missiles punched through Pakistan’s largely Chinese-origin air defence network with devastating accuracy, hitting airbases and military infrastructure. The world watched. Orders accelerated. (Source: New Indian Express)
The Catch: Russia’s Veto Power
Every BrahMos sale has a hidden constraint. The missile is produced by BrahMos Aerospace, a joint venture between DRDO (50.5%) and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyeniya (49.5%). Moscow’s concurrence is required for every third-country sale. Russian Defence Minister Andrey Belousov conveyed approval for the Vietnam and Indonesia deals during talks with Rajnath Singh in December 2024. (Source: New Indian Express)
Export variants are also capped at 290 km under MTCR guidelines, though India — a member since 2016 — has developed extended-range versions beyond 450 km for its own forces. BrahMos Aerospace is working to cut costs by nearly 20% over the next two years while developing the lighter 1.2-tonne BrahMos-NG for wider platform integration. (Source: New Indian Express)
India is targeting ₹50,000 crore in annual defence exports by 2029. The missile that once had no takers is now the calling card.

evening.title: Can Project Kusha Be Used for Land Attack Like Russia’s S-400? Here’s What We Know
evening.text:
As India builds out a multi-layered air defence shield combining the Russian-origin S-400 Triumf with its own indigenous Project Kusha interceptor system, an unusual question keeps surfacing in defence circles: could either of these surface-to-air missile systems double up as a land-attack weapon in a pinch? The answer, it turns out, is more nuanced than a simple yes or no, and understanding it says a lot about how modern air defence missiles actually work, and why India has deliberately kept its ground-strike and air-defence arsenals separate.
The S-400’s Quiet Second Life as a Ground-Attack Weapon
The S-400 Triumf was designed from the ground up as an air defence system, built to shoot down enemy aircraft, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles at long range. But its primary interceptor family, the 48N6 series, has a documented history of being pressed into an entirely different role. Russia has reportedly fired 48N6 missiles from S-400 batteries at ground targets during its war in Ukraine, a use case that falls well outside the system’s original design brief but is technically achievable given how the missile is guided.
The 48N6 relies on inertial navigation with radio command mid-course correction, switching to semi-active or active radar homing only in its terminal phase against airborne targets. When aimed at a fixed ground coordinate instead, the missile essentially flies a ballistic arc to a programmed location and detonates its blast-fragmentation warhead overhead. That’s a meaningfully different proposition from a dedicated land-attack weapon. The warhead is optimised for shredding aircraft in flight, not for penetrating or precisely destroying a ground target, so what you get is closer to an extremely expensive, extremely long-range unguided rocket than anything resembling a precision-guided munition like BrahMos.
Why This Happens: Munition Shortages, Not Doctrine
The pattern behind Russia’s use of S-400 missiles against ground targets tells its own story. Analysts widely view this as a symptom of dedicated land-attack munition shortages rather than a considered doctrinal choice. Firing a surface-to-air interceptor at a ground target ties up a high-value air defence battery, burns through an expensive missile stock that exists to protect against aerial threats, and ultimately delivers a warhead payload far smaller than what a purpose-built ballistic or cruise missile of comparable range would carry. It’s a field expedient, not a preferred tactic, and one that comes with a real opportunity cost: every 48N6 used against a building or a road junction is one less interceptor available the next time an aircraft or missile threatens the battery’s actual coverage zone.
Project Kusha: India’s Answer, Built Strictly for Air Defence
India’s indigenous Project Kusha, currently under development, is designed to fill a similar strategic niche to the S-400, providing long-range air defence against fighter aircraft, cruise missiles, ballistic missiles, UAVs, and other aerial threats. Every publicly available description of the programme frames it exclusively in these air-defence terms; there is no official DRDO disclosure describing a land-attack mode for the system.
Technically, though, “designed for” and “physically capable of” are two different questions. Project Kusha’s interceptors reportedly use a gallium nitride (GaN)-based AESA seeker along with a two-way datalink and inertial navigation with mid-course updates, a guidance architecture broadly similar in principle to what allows the S-400’s 48N6 to be redirected at ground coordinates. Any missile using inertial navigation with mid-course correction is, at its core, solving a trajectory-and-timing problem. Whether the target is an aircraft at altitude or a fixed point on the ground is largely a matter of what coordinates the fire-control software is told to fly toward, and whether the guidance and fusing logic actually support that mode. Nothing about the airframe or seeker inherently rules out a ground-strike capability; it’s the software configuration and warhead design that would need to be adapted, and neither has been disclosed for Kusha.
Same Guidance Logic, Same Warhead Limitation
This is where the comparison between the two systems gets genuinely interesting rather than purely academic. Both systems share the same fundamental limitation if ever repurposed for ground strikes: a blast-fragmentation warhead built to shred aircraft in flight, not to destroy hardened or precise ground targets. Neither the S-400 nor Project Kusha was engineered with a land-attack warhead, guidance mode, or targeting workflow in mind. The S-400’s ground-strike use in Ukraine simply demonstrates that the underlying guidance chain permits it as an improvised, secondary application, not that Russia built a genuine dual-role weapon.
Why India Doesn’t Need Kusha to Do Double Duty
The more strategically relevant point for India is that Project Kusha doesn’t need a land-attack capability, disclosed or otherwise, because India already fields a robust and rapidly expanding surface-to-surface missile arsenal purpose-built for that mission. Systems like BrahMos, Pralay, Shaurya, and Nirbhay are designed from the outset for precision or near-precision land attack, with warheads, guidance packages, and flight profiles optimised specifically for striking ground targets, something a repurposed air-defence interceptor could never match in efficiency or effect.
Keeping these two mission sets, air defence and land attack, doctrinally and operationally separate isn’t a limitation; it’s good military logic. An air defence battery’s entire value lies in its ability to protect airspace continuously. Diverting its limited interceptor stock toward ground strikes, even occasionally, degrades that core mission for a marginal and inefficient land-attack effect that dedicated missiles already deliver far better.
Neither the S-400 nor Project Kusha is, in any meaningful sense, a land-attack weapon. The S-400 has been used that way in the field as a stopgap under wartime munition pressure, while Project Kusha has no disclosed land-attack mode at all, reflecting India’s deliberate choice to keep its air defence and surface-to-surface missile fleets doctrinally distinct. The technical possibility of repurposing either system’s guidance architecture for ground coordinates exists in principle, but the operational logic, and India’s already well-stocked land-attack arsenal, gives it little reason to ever go down that road.

evening.title: IAF’s ASRAAM License-Build Push and Why India Still Needs a Cheaper Close-Combat Missile
evening.text:
The Indian Air Force is planning to obtain a licence to build the British MBDA ASRAAM as its standard close-combat air-to-air missile for an increasing number of aircraft in its fleet, ranging from the Tejas Mk1A to the Su-30MKI and the MiG-29UPG. However, even though ASRAAM is becoming the IAF’s top choice for within-visual-range combat, its cost may lead the service to adopt a separate, less expensive close-combat missile, possibly one based on technology from DRDO’s existing VSHORADS surface-to-air missile rather than one that is completely new.
ASRAAM’s Growing Role Across the IAF Fleet
The story of ASRAAM’s entry into service in India goes back more than ten years. In 2013 the Indian Air Force chose the missile following a competitive assessment of the Israeli Python, Germany’s Diehl IRIS-T and the American Raytheon AIM-9X Sidewinder, the missile eventually winning the Air Force’s New Generation Close Combat Missile (NGCCM) programme. Since that time the integration of the ASRAAM has gradually extended well beyond its initial scope, the missile now being fitted or having been fitted on the Tejas Mk1A, the upgraded Jaguars, the Su-30MKIs and most recently the MiG-29UPG fleet, with the older Russian-made R-73 being replaced on a number of platforms as part of a phased approach.
The missile provides a real improvement on the systems it is replacing. While the R-73 has an engagement range of about 30 km, the ASRAAM has a range of some 50 km, together with a more advanced infrared seeker, better maneuverability, and a high off-boresight targeting ability which allows the missile to acquire targets at very steep angles relative to the launching aircraft – an important asset in close combat situations. Most importantly, in view of India’s aim at self-reliance, the introduction of the ASRAAM also includes local production, since MBDA and Bharat Dynamics Limited have entered into a licensing agreement to set up a final assembly, integration and testing facility at BDL’s Hyderabad manufacturing plant, thus enabling India to carry out local assembly, testing and maintenance rather than depending entirely on imported missiles.
Why Cost Still Becomes the Limiting Factor
Although the ASRAAM has some technical advantages, obtaining a sophisticated, high-off-boresight, imaging-infrared missile from the West is inherently more expensive than choosing older or simpler options. Even though domestic assembly has eased part of the cost burden, the ASRAAM is still a high-end weapon, and the IAF’s fighter fleet is both large and increasing, including the Tejas Mk1A and Mk2, the Su-30MKI, the Rafale, the MiG-29UPG, and eventually the AMCA. It would not be economically viable to equip every single close-combat weapon loadout on every sortie of that entire fleet with a missile costing as much as the ASRAAM, unlike the case with a cheaper complementary missile.
It is in this area that the general reasoning which has already influenced the IAF’s approach regarding other types of munitions—such as cheap countermeasures for cheap threats and low-cost interceptors for saturation situations—begins to be applied to within-visual-range air combat as well. It is not necessary for every close-combat engagement to make use of the full capabilities of the ASRAAM; in the case of training flights, lower-threat situations, and when cost-sensitive procurement decisions are being made, there is a advantage in having a more economical missile available together with the more expensive one, and this alternative is used selectively rather than exclusively.
The VSHORADS Connection: A Ready-Made Technology Base
It is exactly in this area that DRDO’s Very Short Range Air Defence System (VSHORADS) takes on strategic interest, not as a direct replacement for the ASRAAM, but as a possible foundation for a truly low-cost air-to-air missile intended for close combat. The VSHORADS is a fourth-generation, man-portable air defence system developed at DRDO’s Research Centre Imarat and was originally designed to deal with low-altitude aerial threats such as drones, helicopters, and aircraft at short range. The system is based on a miniaturised reaction control system, integrated avionics, and a dual-waveband imaging infrared seeker—technologies which have already been proven successful through a number of flight tests carried out at the Integrated Test Range in Chandipur, during which the missile managed to intercept high-speed aerial targets under a variety of engagement scenarios.
VSHORADS is small when compared to other missiles, having a weight of about 20.5 kg, a length of 2 metres and a 90 mm diameter, and it is powered by a dual-thrust solid rocket motor which allows it to reach speeds of up to Mach 1.5, with an effective range of approximately 6 to 8 km according to the particular variant. The size and cost characteristics, which were designed for mass production as a shoulder-fired weapon used by infantry rather than as a high-end weapon for fighter jets, are precisely the kind of basis that can be adapted for use when launched from an aircraft. The fundamental sensor and guidance technology—the imaging infrared seeker with a decent level of resistance to countermeasures—already exists and has already been demonstrated in flight; all that would then have to be done is to re-engineer the airframe, the launch rail interface, and the aerodynamic surfaces for use when mounted on an aircraft rather than for shoulder-launching from the ground.
Why This Approach Makes Strategic Sense
Designing a low-cost close-combat missile on the basis of the already-established VSHORADS technology, rather than launching a completely new development programme, would enable DRDO and its industrial partners to make use of seeker technology, guidance algorithms, and production facilities which have already passed through numerous successful trial campaigns. Since VSHORADS was originally developed with domestic mass production and cost efficiency for general infantry use in mind, this same approach to production could result in considerably lower unit costs for an air-to-air version as compared to one based on a completely new design.
This is an example of a trend that is already being seen in other areas of India’s air combat modernisation: instead of believing that each type of weapon needs a single, uniformly top-quality solution, the Indian Air Force and DRDO seem to be moving towards having a tiered arsenal, comprising a top-end system that is imported or assembled under licence such as ASRAAM for the most demanding situations, together with a cheaper, indigenously developed option for higher-volume or lower-intensity operations. It is the same kind of cost asymmetry that has already led the IAF to show interest in low-cost interceptors for dealing with inexpensive drone threats and may now be extending to the close-combat air-to-air missile area as well.

evening.title: The Chip at the Heart of Every Weapon: India’s Race for Semiconductor Sovereignty
evening.text:
Every AI-enabled military system, every AESA radar, every electronic warfare suite, every guided missile, every drone navigation system, and every encrypted communication link depends on a component that India imports 90-95% of: the semiconductor chip. A nation that does not control its semiconductor supply chain does not truly control its weapons systems. This is the strategic vulnerability that almost no one in Indian defence journalism is writing about — and it is closing faster than most people realise.
The Rafale refusal that started everything
The story begins with a refusal. In 2016, during the Rafale fighter jet negotiations with France, India pushed hard for the transfer of Gallium Nitride (GaN) technology under the contract’s mandatory 50% offset clause. Paris declined, citing export controls and the technology’s strategic sensitivity. France was willing to deliver state-of-the-art hardware, but the “recipe” behind the semiconductor heart of modern radars and electronic warfare systems remained off-limits.
DRDO’s response was to build it from scratch. The Solid State Physics Laboratory in Delhi and the GAETEC facility in Hyderabad were tasked with mastering the entire GaN technology cycle — from material growth and wafer fabrication to system-level integration. By March 2023, they had produced GaN-based Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuits (MMICs) at laboratory level. In January 2026, DRDO declared its indigenous GaN technology “fully operational,” making India one of only seven nations with end-to-end sovereign GaN capability.
The FermionIC breakthrough: Indian chips in Indian radars
The most significant development in Indian defence semiconductor history happened almost entirely outside the headlines. FermionIC Design, an Indian semiconductor startup, has developed GaN-based chips that are being qualified to power the Transmit-Receive Modules (TRMs) of the Virupaksha AESA radar for the Su-30MKI “Super Sukhoi” upgrade. With approximately 2,400 TRMs, Virupaksha is among the most powerful fighter radars under development globally.
This is not a laboratory curiosity. These chips have undergone rigorous validation meeting or exceeding performance benchmarks typically associated with Tier-1 global semiconductor suppliers. For decades, critical components such as radar semiconductors were sourced from foreign vendors, creating dependencies that could become vulnerabilities during geopolitical crises. By integrating indigenously designed GaN chips into a frontline fighter radar, India moves closer to a fully sovereign supply chain for advanced military electronics.
The strategic implications extend beyond performance. Using Indian-designed chips eliminates the risk of hidden vulnerabilities, backdoors, or external supply chain compromises. It ensures that sensitive mission data, targeting information, and real-time battlefield updates remain fully under national control. As one analyst noted: “In wartime, no external supplier can switch us off. That changes the calculus entirely.”
RISC-V and the DHRUV64: the processor nobody noticed
Parallel to the GaN programme, India is building an indigenous processor ecosystem on the open-source RISC-V architecture, which requires zero licensing fees and offers complete design freedom. C-DAC launched DHRUV64 (VEGA AS2161) — India’s first fully indigenous 64-bit microprocessor — designed for 5G, automotive, IoT, and defence applications. It is explicitly positioned as a “secure processor for defence applications” free from foreign backdoors and supply chain vulnerabilities.
This sits within a broader portfolio including SHAKTI, AJIT, VIKRAM, and THEJAS processors, with DHANUSH and DHANUSH+ System-on-Chips variants in development. The Cabinet approved ₹1.27 lakh crore for Semicon Mission 2.0 in July 2026, with provisions to incentivise even suppliers of raw materials — minerals and gases — in the chip manufacturing chain.
The military LLM vulnerability
A CLAWS analysis published in July 2026 flagged a deeper risk: India’s growing use of military AI systems built on foreign semiconductor and cloud infrastructure creates structural vulnerabilities that could compromise long-term military autonomy. As AI systems like Anthropic’s Project Glasswing demonstrate the ability to independently identify and assess software vulnerabilities, India’s reliance on foreign-designed chips, frontier AI ecosystems, and cloud infrastructure creates a sovereignty gap. The chips may work, but if the underlying architecture, training data, and cloud services are foreign-controlled, “sovereignty” is an illusion. The CLAWS paper argues for a sovereignty-centred framework integrating indigenous AI systems, semiconductor self-reliance, and sovereign compute infrastructure.
The fab gap that remains
Despite design breakthroughs, India still has no operational semiconductor fabrication facility producing advanced chips. The Tata Electronics fab in Dholera, Gujarat (₹91,000 crore investment) is under construction. Micron’s ATMP facility in Sanand is being built. Renesas’s OSAT facility is operational at pilot scale, with first chips expected mid-2026. But the gap between designing a chip and manufacturing it at scale is enormous. India’s NITI Aayog report explicitly identifies the need for “secure fabs and packaging lines with air-gapped networks and controlled supply chains” for “defence, aerospace and strategic infrastructure chips” including radiation-hardened, high-reliability, and tamper-resistant devices. These are not commercial fabs; they are dedicated, classified facilities that do not yet exist in India.
What France refused to transfer under the Rafale deal has now been built indigenously — at the chip design level. What remains is the manufacturing infrastructure to produce those designs at the scale and security classification that defence requires. The next decade will determine whether India’s semiconductor sovereignty moves from design to fabrication, or remains a story of brilliant engineering without the industrial base to match.

evening.title: An-32: A Flying Relic that needs to go soon from IAF
evening.text:
On 13 June 2026, an Indian Air Force An-32 transport aircraft of 43 Squadron crashed at Jorhat airbase in Assam during a routine landing. The aircraft had taken off earlier that morning, developed a technical fault, and returned. While taxiing after landing, it skidded off the runway, overturned in a grassy area, and exploded. Five personnel were killed: Squadron Leader Prashant Singh, Flight Lieutenant Shubham Kumar, Sergeant Jitendra Sharma, Agniveervayu Khemaram Kumawat, and Agniveervayu Danish Alam. A co-pilot survived with injuries. (Source: New Indian Express, 13 June 2026; idrw.org, 13 June 2026; India Sentinels, 13 June 2026)
The story that broke hearts across India was that of Agniveer Khemaram Kumawat. He was 22 years old, from Panchota village in Rajasthan’s Didwana-Kuchaman district. He had joined the IAF under the Agnipath scheme in December 2022 and was nearing the end of his four-year tenure. His family had already begun marriage discussions. “Wedding discussions had already begun at home. We never imagined such heartbreaking news would arrive instead,” his cousin Mahesh Kumawat said. (Source: New Kerala, 13 June 2026; The Hans India, 14 June 2026)
The An-32: A Flying Relic
The An-32 is a twin-engine Soviet-era military transport aircraft that has been extensively used by the IAF for logistics, cargo transportation, and operational support across diverse terrains, including high-altitude and remote regions. The type has been in service for decades, and despite mid-life upgrades, its safety record has been a persistent concern. (Source: India Sentinels)
The most notorious previous incident was the disappearance of an An-32 over the Bay of Bengal in July 2016 with 29 personnel on board. Its wreckage was eventually located at a depth of approximately 3,400 metres. The Jorhat crash came just months after another IAF tragedy in Assam — a Sukhoi Su-30MKI fighter jet crash in Karbi Anglong district on 5 March 2026 that killed both pilots. (Source: India Sentinels; idrw.org)
The Agniveer Tragedy Deepens
The deaths of the two Agniveervayus in the An-32 crash came amid a firestorm over the treatment of Agniveers killed in action. Just a month earlier, in July 2026, Scroll published a devastating investigation into the family of Agniveer Muralinaik, who was killed in cross-border shelling on 9 May 2025 during Operation Sindoor at the age of 24. His mother, Jyothibai, filed a petition in the Bombay High Court demanding the same lifelong pension, health insurance, and welfare benefits provided to families of regular soldiers killed in action. (Source: Scroll, 14 July 2026)
The government’s response was blunt. In an affidavit filed on 6 May 2026, the Centre told the Bombay High Court that Agniveers are “not similarly situated” as regular soldiers and cannot claim pension parity. “There can be no parity between two differently placed classes of persons,” the affidavit stated. The government confirmed Muralinaik’s family received approximately ₹2.3 crore in compensation — insurance plus severance — but no lifelong pension. (Source: Times of India, 11 May 2026; Rediff, 11 May 2026; Law Trend, 11 May 2026)
The petition argues: “Soldiers fighting shoulder-to-shoulder cannot be treated differently in death.” The case rests on Article 14 of the Constitution, which guarantees the right to equality. The Bombay High Court reprimanded the government for delaying its response and warned of heavy fines. The matter is pending. (Source: Scroll; Media India, 15 May 2026)
Meanwhile, on 1 August 2026, a 20-year-old youth named Gokul collapsed and died during an Agniveer recruitment endurance run at the Indira Gandhi Sports Complex in Puducherry. He was rushed to the Government General Hospital where doctors could not save him. (Source: The Hindu, 1 August 2026)
From recruitment to death in service, the Agniveer programme is generating headlines that no amount of government spin can contain.

evening.title: Former BJP MP Kirit Somaiya seeks SEBI probe into sharp Sensex swing during CAS
evening.text: Kirit Somaiya, former Member of the Lok Sabha and vice president of the Bharatiya Janata Party's Maharashtra unit, has sought the Securities and Exchange Board of India's (SEBI) attention over the sharp swings in the Sensex during the Closing Auction Session (CAS) on August 27.The Sensex plunged more than 2,000 points within minutes during the CAS on Thursday, falling from around 77,200 at 3:17 pm to nearly 74,983 at 3:23 pm. The index subsequently recovered some of its losses but still ended the day 539 points, or 0.7%, lower at 76,934.India changed how closing prices are determined from August 3. Instead of calculating the close using the volume-weighted average price (VWAP) during the final half-hour of trading, exchanges introduced a short Closing Auction Session, in which buy and sell orders are aggregated, and a single equilibrium price is discovered.In a communication seeking attention to the August 27 movement, Somaiya asked whether the sharp intra-session swing pointed to a weakness in the CAS mechanism and called for an inquiry and action."On 27 August, during the last 12 minutes of trading at NSE/BSE, the Sensex crashed over 2,200 points and then recovered 2,000 points," Somaiya said, asking whether "it is a weakness in the CAS system".He also asked whether the move could have been linked to any deliberate attempt to undermine the implementation of CAS, while calling on SEBI to examine the matter."SEBI must not take this CASUALLY," he said. "If it is a weakness, then the officials who drafted it should owe an explanation. If it is done knowingly, is it healthy? Is it sabotage to stop implementation of CAS?""Shockingly, such things happened during the process of having a healthy system," Somaiya said, adding that he wanted "not only inquiry but action also."Liquidity concerns after 3:15 pmAlong with his communication, Somaiya shared an observation that attributed the sharp movement partly to a lack of liquidity after 3:15 pm."The fundamental problem is also - there is no depth due to lack of liquidity after 3.15. All now trade before 3.15 pm. Any person who wants to purchase/sale after 3.15 pm doesn't find liquidity and hence volatility," the observation said.The accompanying note proposed temporarily suspending CAS and reintroducing it after a redesign, citing several concerns around liquidity, price discovery and the interaction between the cash and derivatives markets.Under the present framework, continuous trading in CAS securities ends at 3:15 p.m., after which the market moves into a separate auction. Equity derivatives, however, continue to trade until 3:40 p.m.The note argues that this structure removes continuous-market liquidity before the auction begins. At 3:15 p.m., the continuous price-discovery mechanism is stopped and replaced by the auction order book, which the note describes as materially shallower.Separate auctions on NSE, BSEThe note also raises concerns about the fragmentation of closing liquidity between NSE and BSE. It points out that the same security can undergo separate closing auctions on the two exchanges, with separate order books, imbalances and potentially different equilibrium prices.According to the note, on the first day of CAS, reported auction turnover was approximately Rs 1,276 crore on NSE compared with around Rs 10.8 crore on BSE, a difference of more than 100 times.It argues that while the purpose of a closing auction is to concentrate liquidity, separate auctions on the two exchanges could instead fragment liquidity.Questions over closing-price formationThe note also questions whether a relatively small amount of auction trading can provide a sufficiently robust price for a much larger pool of capital whose value is determined using the official closing price.The closing price feeds into mutual fund NAVs, portfolio valuations, index closing levels, passive-fund tracking, mark-to-market valuations, derivative settlement economics and performance measurement, according to the note.It therefore argues that the framework should consider minimum liquidity and market-quality conditions before an auction price automatically becomes the official close.Another concern relates to the CAS's ±3% auction band. The note argues that such a range could result in a significant change in the marked-to-market value of large companies even when the quantity actually matched in the auction represents only a small portion of the company's outstanding shares.For a company with a Rs 5 lakh crore market capitalisation, the note estimates that a 3% movement would change its marked market capitalisation by approximately Rs 15,000 crore.It proposes a more conservative, dynamic collar that expands only when supported by substantial two-sided auction liquidity.Cash and derivatives operate on different timelinesThe note further highlights the different trading timelines for the cash and derivatives markets. While continuous cash trading for CAS securities stops at 3:15 p.m., equity derivatives continue trading beyond the auction.According to the note, this means futures and options can continue to reflect changing information and expectations even after the underlying cash security has ceased continuous price discovery.It argues that this weakens the normal cash-futures arbitrage mechanism at the point when the official closing benchmark is being established.Concern over thin liquidity and expiry-day volatilityThe note also argues that inadequate CAS liquidity could create a self-reinforcing cycle. If large institutions perceive liquidity in the auction as insufficient, they may execute before 3:15 p.m., further reducing auction liquidity. Lower liquidity could then increase price impact and execution uncertainty, discouraging participation further.The note calls this a “negative liquidity flywheel”: low liquidity increases auction impact, weakens execution certainty, reduces participation and further drains liquidity.“Participation is therefore partly an outcome of good market design, not merely aprerequisite that can be assumed to emerge over time,” it said.(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views and opinions given by the experts are their own. These do not represent the views of Economic Times)
